headline: Semantic Cache Makes Free LLM Quotas Feel Infinite
summary: A new caching technique can cut token consumption by roughly half, effectively doubling the utility of free LLM tiers.
details: Most developers treat LLM token allowances as a budget, but a semantic cache offers a more efficient model. By storing and reusing responses to rephrased requests, this cache can cut token consumption by approximately 50% in typical agent loops, making free tiers feel practically limitless.

MonkeyCode's free offering includes a 10-million-token allowance and a free server, making quota efficiency a critical concern. This article details a working, zero-dependency implementation of a semantic cache, along with the threshold tuning necessary for production prototypes.

Developer logs reveal that agent workloads often involve semantically similar prompts, with roughly 35% of requests being near-duplicates. Sending these duplicates burns tokens, adds latency, and risks inconsistent answers. The solution is to prevent these duplicate calls from reaching the LLM.

A semantic cache intercepts incoming prompts, calculates a similarity score against cached prompts using character n-gram Jaccard similarity, and returns a stored response if the score exceeds a set threshold. This reduces calls to the LLM without compromising quality for novel requests, making the system cheaper and faster over time.

The core challenge is determining prompt similarity. While embedding models are common, a zero-dependency alternative using character trigrams (overlapping three-character shingles) is effective for short prompts. Threshold tuning, calibrated against manually labeled prompt pairs, is crucial for balancing hit rate and accuracy.

A cache requires an eviction policy to prevent memory leaks. The prototype uses SQLite with a one-hour time-to-live (TTL) and a hit counter. Entries with lower hit counts and older creation times are prioritized for eviction when the cache exceeds its size limit, ensuring it remains focused on frequently recurring prompts.

headline: Twitch and Amazon sued for using streamer content to train AI
summary: A class action lawsuit alleges that Twitch and Amazon used streamer content for AI training without consent or licensing, potentially breaching contracts and causing financial harm to creators.
details: A class action lawsuit has been filed against Twitch and Amazon, accusing the companies of using streamer content to train AI models without obtaining proper consent or licensing.
The lawsuit, initiated by streamer Warren Pandiscia, claims that Twitch and Amazon utilized his streams and videos as a dataset for Amazon's AI products without permission.
This action allegedly constitutes a breach of contract, as the companies are accused of using streamers as "free training stock for separate commercial AI products."

The complaint further states that Twitch and Amazon have profited from their streamers, who have consequently "lost money or property as a result of defendants' unlawful, unfair and fraudulent practices."

Twitch recently introduced an opt-out option for AI training, but the lawsuit highlights that the default setting was opt-in, with a company executive suggesting that "if it was opt-in, nobody would opt in."
